# Stop Correcting AI Code. Build the System Agents Need.

## The Real Problem Isn't the AI — It's Your Workflow

Most teams using AI coding assistants have fallen into the same trap: they treat the AI like a junior developer who needs constant supervision. Review every line. Fix the obvious mistakes. Push back on the weird patterns. Rinse, repeat.

That's not a sustainable model. It's also not where this is heading.

The harder question — the one most engineering orgs haven't seriously asked — is whether you should be building systems that make AI correction unnecessary in the first place.

---

## What's Actually Happening

The conversation around AI-assisted development is shifting. The early excitement was about generation speed: "Look how fast it writes code." The second wave was about quality concerns: "But the code has bugs and security holes." Now we're entering a third phase that's less obvious but more consequential.

The New Stack recently published a piece arguing that the corrective loop — human reviews AI output, human fixes AI output, human re-prompts AI — is fundamentally the wrong approach at scale. The argument isn't that AI code is good enough to skip review. It's that the review-and-fix model doesn't scale, doesn't teach the AI anything, and burns human attention on repetitive work.

The alternative framing: instead of correcting AI agents after the fact, build the systems and guardrails that shape what agents produce in the first place. Shift left on AI output quality, the same way we shifted left on security testing a decade ago.

This means treating AI agents less like team members who need coaching and more like automated systems that need proper constraints, feedback loops, and environmental controls. The same way you wouldn't manually review every CI build — you'd set up automated tests and quality gates — you shouldn't manually review every AI-generated function.

The piece points to a fundamental tension: human attention is the bottleneck. If your AI assistant generates code 10x faster than a human, but a human still has to review 100% of it, you haven't actually saved engineering time. You've just moved the bottleneck from writing to reviewing.

---

## Why Practitioners Should Care

### The Correction Tax Is Real

Every team I've talked to that's adopted AI coding tools has some version of the same complaint: "It's fast, but I spend so much time fixing the output that I'm not sure I'm ahead."

That's the correction tax. And it compounds.

When you correct AI output manually, you're doing several things that don't scale:
- Spending senior engineer time on junior-level review tasks
- Not capturing your corrections in any reusable form
- Training yourself to distrust the tool without training the tool to earn your trust
- Creating implicit knowledge about "what works" that stays in your head

The correction tax also has a security dimension. When engineers are fatigued from reviewing AI-generated code, they start skimming. They approve things they shouldn't. The volume of output overwhelms the review capacity, and gaps open up.

### The "System" Framing Changes Everything

The shift from "correct the agent" to "build the system" is a meaningful reframe. It asks different questions:

**Instead of:** "How do I fix this AI-generated code?"  
**Ask:** "What constraints would have prevented this output?"

**Instead of:** "How do I prompt it better?"  
**Ask:** "What context does it need automatically, without me typing it every time?"

**Instead of:** "How do I catch this bug in review?"  
**Ask:** "What automated check would catch this before I ever see it?"

This is familiar territory for anyone who's worked in DevSecOps. We learned years ago that "review harder" doesn't scale. You build pipelines. You automate checks. You fail fast. You make the secure path the easy path.

The same principles apply to AI-generated code. The goal isn't to become a better AI code reviewer. The goal is to build systems where most AI output is either correct by construction or rejected automatically before it reaches you.

### Guardrails Over Guidance

There's a difference between guidance and guardrails.

Guidance is telling the AI "please follow our coding standards" in the prompt. It's hoping the AI remembers your architecture preferences. It's adding context that may or may not get weighted appropriately.

Guardrails are automated gates that enforce requirements. Static analysis that fails the build. Schema validation that rejects malformed output. Integration tests that catch behavioral regressions. Security scanners that block vulnerable patterns.

Guidance is advisory. Guardrails are structural.

The teams getting the most value from AI coding tools are the ones investing in guardrails, not the ones writing better prompts. They're treating AI output as untrusted-by-default and building the infrastructure to verify it automatically.

### The Security Angle

From a security perspective, this reframe is critical.

AI-generated code has known vulnerability patterns. It tends to be overly permissive with inputs. It often generates code that looks secure but has subtle flaws — SQL queries that use parameterization incorrectly, authentication checks that have bypass conditions, error handling that leaks information.

If your security model is "engineers will catch these in review," you're in trouble. Review fatigue is real. Volume is increasing. The attack surface grows with every AI-generated commit.

The alternative is building security guardrails that treat AI output the same way you'd treat untrusted third-party code:

- SAST scans on every AI-generated file, not just on PR
- Dependency checks that flag AI-introduced packages
- Runtime guardrails that limit what AI-generated code can access
- Automated tests that specifically target common AI vulnerability patterns

This isn't about distrusting AI. It's about trusting systems over attention.

---

## Building the System: What It Actually Looks Like

So what does "building the system agents need" look like in practice? Based on what's emerging, here are the key components:

### 1. Context Injection, Not Context Prompting

Instead of relying on engineers to provide context in every prompt, build systems that automatically inject relevant context. This might include:

- Current file structure and dependencies
- Team coding standards as machine-readable rules
- Security requirements for the domain
- Recent commits and architectural decisions

The goal is to give the AI the information it needs to produce correct output without human intervention. The less you have to type in the prompt, the more consistent the output.

### 2. Automated Quality Gates

Every AI-generated code path should pass through automated quality gates before human review. These gates should include:

- Linting and formatting (non-negotiable)
- Static analysis for bugs and security issues
- Test coverage requirements
- Architecture conformance checks

If the AI output fails any gate, it doesn't reach a human. It either gets rejected or regenerated. Human attention is reserved for code that's already passed basic quality checks.

### 3. Feedback Loops That Actually Loop

When humans do correct AI output, those corrections should feed back into the system. This might mean:

- Logging correction patterns to identify systematic issues
- Updating prompts or context based on common fixes
- Training custom models or fine-tuning on your codebase [UNVERIFIED — capability varies by tool]
- Building team-specific rules that catch repeated errors

The worst outcome is correcting the same AI mistake a hundred times without ever updating the system to prevent it.

### 4. Scoped Authority

Not all AI-generated code should have the same level of trust. Building a system means defining scopes:

- What can the AI generate without review?
- What requires human approval?
- What is off-limits entirely?

This might map to risk levels. AI can generate unit tests freely. AI can generate business logic with review. AI cannot modify authentication code without security team approval.

Scoped authority reduces the review burden while maintaining control over high-risk areas.

---

## [CHRIS TAKE]

---

## What to Watch / What to Do Next

### What to Watch

**Tool evolution:** The major AI coding assistants are starting to build some of these system-level capabilities natively. GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and others are adding context awareness and integration features. Watch for tools that treat "system building" as a first-class feature, not an afterthought.

**Pipeline integration maturity:** The gap between "AI generates code" and "AI-generated code flows through a proper pipeline" is still wide at most organizations. Watch for better integration patterns and reference architectures.

**Security tooling adaptation:** SAST and SCA tools are starting to adapt to AI-generated code patterns. Some are adding rules specifically for common AI coding mistakes. This is an area where tooling is behind the curve but catching up.

**Organizational models:** Some teams are experimenting with dedicated roles for AI system design — engineers who focus on building the scaffolding around AI tools rather than using them directly. Whether this becomes a common pattern is worth watching.

### What to Do Next

**Audit your correction patterns.** For one week, track every correction you make to AI-generated code. Look for patterns. If you're fixing the same types of issues repeatedly, that's a system problem, not a review problem.

**Invest in automated gates.** If AI-generated code is reaching human reviewers without passing basic automated checks, you're wasting human attention. Prioritize getting those gates in place.

**Define your trust boundaries.** Where is AI-generated code acceptable with minimal review? Where does it require scrutiny? Where is it off-limits? Having explicit answers makes the system work.

**Capture feedback systematically.** When you correct AI output, log it somewhere. Build a corpus of corrections that can inform prompt engineering, custom rules, or tool configuration.

**Treat AI security as a distinct workstream.** AI-generated code has different risk patterns than human-written code. Your security approach should reflect that. This might mean different SAST rules, different review protocols, or different testing strategies.

---

## Closing Question

Here's what I keep coming back to: most teams are still in the "correct and repeat" cycle with AI tools, and most of them know it's not sustainable. But building the system — the guardrails, the context injection, the automated gates — requires upfront investment that's hard to justify when you're already shipping features.

So the question is: **At what point does the correction tax become high enough that building the system is obviously the right investment?** And are you tracking the right metrics to even know when you've crossed that threshold?
